a: and that he will not wipe out the whole earth
t: "Not wipe out," or "when he wipes out"?
p: Dillmann has a negative; the EOTC text does not.

readings.w: Dillmann's Ge'ez text (1851)
readings.orig: ወኢይደምስሳ ፡ ለኵላ ፡ ምድር (wäʾiydämsəsa läkʷila mədr)
readings.en: and that he not destroy the whole earth
readings.plain: and that he will not wipe out the whole earth

readings.w: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church printed text (EOTC)
readings.orig: ወይደመስሳ ፡ ለኵላ ፡ ምድር (wäydämässa läkʷəla mədr)
readings.en: and he will destroy the whole earth
readings.plain: even when he wipes out the whole earth

why: Dillmann's negative fits Enoch's prayer in 84:5, which asks God not to destroy all flesh. The EOTC wording can be read as "a remnant may be left when he destroys the earth," which also makes sense, since the Flood does come.

a: so that the destruction lasts forever
p: Dillmann: "and there would be destruction forever." EOTC: "and let there be no destruction forever."

readings.w: Dillmann's Ge'ez text (1851)
readings.orig: ወይከውን ፡ ሐጒል ፡ ለዓለም (wäykäwn ḥägʷil läʿaläm)
readings.en: and there would be destruction forever
readings.plain: so that the destruction lasts forever

readings.w: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church printed text (EOTC)
readings.orig: ወኢይኩን ፡ ሀጕል ፡ ለዓለም (wäʾiykun ḥägʷil läʿaläm)
readings.en: and let there not be destruction forever
readings.plain: and let there be no destruction that lasts forever

why: Both say the same thing in the end. Dillmann's text states what would follow if God emptied the earth; the EOTC turns it into one more request. The Plain English Translation follows Dillmann, as Charles does.

p: The EOTC list of birds adds "eagles" after the falcons.

readings.w: Dillmann's Ge'ez text (1851)
readings.orig: ወሲሲተ ፡ ወአውስተ (wäsisitä wäʾäwsətä)
readings.en: falcons and vultures
readings.plain: falcons, vultures

readings.w: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church printed text (EOTC)
readings.orig: ወሲሲተ ፡ አንስርተ ፡ ወአውስተ (wäsisitä ʾänsərtä wäʾäwsətä)
readings.en: falcons, eagles and vultures
readings.plain: falcons, eagles, vultures

why: Dillmann's shorter list is followed. The EOTC adds ʾänsərt, the word used for the eagles that lead the birds in 90:2, perhaps to make this list match that one. Both lists then also have fonqas, which Charles also rendered "eagles." The EOTC also puts wolves before dogs.

a: the Lord of the sheep raised up another sheep from among them
t: Did the Lord raise up the ram?
p: The Vatican Greek says the Lord of the sheep raised up the ram. The EOTC text says the sheep simply arose.

readings.w: Vatican Greek fragment (Byzantine shorthand), ed. Mai, deciphered by Gildemeister (1855), as printed by Charles (1893); Dillmann's bracketed words [ʾƎgziʾä ʾäbagʿ]
readings.orig: μέχρι οὗ ἤγειρεν ὁ κύριος τῶν προβάτων κριὸν ἕνα ἐκ τῶν προβάτων
readings.en: until the Lord of the sheep raised up one ram from the sheep
readings.plain: the Lord of the sheep raised up another sheep from among them

readings.w: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church printed text (EOTC); Dillmann's text without his bracketed words reads the same, with the numeral ፩ for ʾäḥädu
readings.orig: ተንሥአ ፡ ካልእ ፡ በግዕ ፡ አሐዱ ፡ እምኔሆሙ (tänśəʾä kalʾ bägʿ ʾäḥädu ʾəmnehomu)
readings.en: another sheep arose, one of them
readings.plain: another sheep rose up from among them

why: The Greek is older than the Ethiopic, and it has the Lord of the sheep raise the ram, as Dillmann's bracketed words also say (Charles's English follows this too). The Plain English Translation follows the Greek for who acts and the Ethiopic for the rest ("another sheep ... who led them"), which the shorter Greek summary lacks.

a: until he had destroyed them all
t: All of them, or many boars?
p: The Greek lists the ram's victims in turn: foxes, then boars ("many"), then the dogs.

readings.w: Dillmann's Ge'ez text (1851); EOTC
readings.orig: እስከ ፡ ለኵሎሙ ፡ አህጐሎሙ (ʾəskä läkʷilomu ʾähgʷälomu)
readings.en: until he destroyed all of them
readings.plain: until he had destroyed them all

readings.w: Vatican Greek fragment (Byzantine shorthand), ed. Mai, deciphered by Gildemeister (1855), as printed by Charles (1893)
readings.orig: καὶ ἐνετίνασσεν εἰς τοὺς ἀλώπεκας καὶ μετ’ αὐτοὺς εἰς τοὺς ὗας καὶ ἀπώλεσεν ὗας πολλοὺς καὶ μετ’ αὐτοὺς ... τοὺς κύνας
readings.en: and he charged at the foxes, and after them at the boars, and destroyed many boars, and after them ... the dogs
readings.plain: charging first at the foxes, then at the boars, destroying many boars, and after them the dogs

why: The Greek is older but is a summary with a lost word, so the Plain English Translation keeps the complete Ethiopic. The Greek's "many boars ... and after them ... the dogs" is less sweeping than the Ethiopic "destroyed them all," and fits better with 89:47, where the dogs (the Philistines) bring Saul down.

a: The ram gave up his glory. He began to butt those sheep and trample them, and he behaved in a shameful way.
p: Ethiopic: Saul gave up his glory and trampled the sheep. Greek: he left his way and walked off the road.

readings.w: Dillmann's Ge'ez text (1851); EOTC
readings.orig: ዘኀደገ ፡ ስብሐቶ ... ወሖረ ፡ ዘእንበለ ፡ ተድላ (zäḫädägä səbḥäto ... wäḥorä zäʾnəbälä tädla)
readings.en: which abandoned its glory, began to butt those sheep, trampled them, and went without seemliness
readings.plain: The ram gave up his glory. He began to butt those sheep and trample them, and he behaved in a shameful way.

readings.w: Vatican Greek fragment (Byzantine shorthand), ed. Mai, deciphered by Gildemeister (1855), as printed by Charles (1893)
readings.orig: ἕως οὗ ἀφῆκεν τὴν ὁδὸν αὐτοῦ καὶ ἤρξατο πορεύεσθαι ἀνοδίᾳ
readings.en: until it left its way and began to walk where there was no road
readings.plain: Then the ram left his way and began to walk where there was no road.

why: Both say Saul went wrong. The Greek "walk where there was no road" stands where the Ethiopic has "went without seemliness," so the two go back to one text. The Greek summary drops the trampling, so the Plain English Translation keeps the fuller Ethiopic. The Greek "way" fits the vision's theme of the path (89:32) and is repeated in its 89:45, so it may well be the older wording.

a: That ram fathered many sheep and fell asleep. Then a little sheep became ram in his place, and he became ruler and leader of those sheep.
p: The Ethiopic has David's death and Solomon here. The Greek goes straight on to 89:49 without them.

readings.w: Dillmann's Ge'ez text (1851); all Ethiopic manuscripts (the EOTC text reads ወዝ ፡ ሐርጌ ፡ ደኃራዊ, "this last ram", with the same sense)
readings.orig: ወዝኩ ፡ ሐርጌ ፡ ወለደ ፡ አባግዐ ፡ ብዙኃነ ፡ ወሰከበ ... (wäzku ḥärge wälädä ʾäbagʿä bəzuḫanä wäsäkäbä ...)
readings.en: and that ram fathered many sheep and fell asleep, and a little sheep became ram in his place...
readings.plain: That ram fathered many sheep and fell asleep. Then a little sheep became ram in his place, and he became ruler and leader of those sheep.

readings.w: Vatican Greek fragment (Byzantine shorthand), ed. Mai, deciphered by Gildemeister (1855), as printed by Charles (1893); Charles printed the sentence after 89:49
readings.orig: Καὶ ὁ κριὸς ὁ δεύτερος ἀναπηδήσας ἀφηγήσατο τῶν προβάτων. Καὶ τὰ πρόβατα ηὐξήθησαν ...
readings.en: And the second ram leapt up and led the sheep. And the sheep grew ...

why: The Plain English Translation keeps the sentence where all Ethiopic manuscripts have it. The Greek supports Charles's view that it stood after 89:49, since it passes straight from 89:48 to 89:49, but the Greek breaks off after 89:49, so we cannot see whether it had the sentence there.

a: whether they went into that house or not
p: The EOTC text adds "or whether they did not go in."

readings.w: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church printed text (EOTC)
readings.orig: ለእመ ፡ ይበውኡ ፡ ኀበ ፡ ዝኩ ፡ ቤት ፡ ወለእመ ፡ ኢይበውኡ (läʾmä yəbäwʾu ḫäbä zəku bet wäläʾmä ʾiybäwʾu)
readings.en: whether they went into that house or did not go in
readings.plain: whether they went into that house or not

readings.w: Dillmann's Ge'ez text (1851)
readings.orig: ለእመ ፡ ይበውኡ ፡ ኀበ ፡ ዝኩ ፡ ቤት (läʾmä yəbäwʾu ḫäbä zəku bet)
readings.en: whether they went into that house
readings.plain: whether they went into that house

why: The meaning is the same. The EOTC's fuller wording makes the Ge'ez question clearer in English, so the Plain English Translation follows it here.

p: The Ethiopic says 37. The arithmetic of 90:5 needs 35, and most scholars correct it.

readings.w: Dillmann's Ge'ez text (1851) and Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church printed text (EOTC); the Ethiopic manuscripts
readings.orig: Dillmann ፴ወ፯ኖላውያን; EOTC ሠላሳ፡ ወሰብዐቱ፡ ኖላውያን (śälasa wäsäbʿätu nolawyan)
readings.en: thirty-seven shepherds
readings.plain: thirty-seven shepherds

readings.w: Correction by R. H. Charles (1912), followed by most modern translators; no manuscript has it
readings.en: thirty-five shepherds
readings.plain: thirty-five shepherds

why: The Plain English Translation translates what the Ethiopic manuscripts say, since no older witness survives for this verse. But the correction is very likely right: 12 shepherds (89:72) plus 23 makes 35, and 35 plus 23 makes the 58 periods of 90:5. Thirty-seven may come from a copyist's slip in the numerals.

a: a word, and that word became a great animal
t: A word, a lamb or a wild ox?
p: Every Ethiopic copy says "word." Charles read "lamb"; others propose "wild ox."

readings.w: Dillmann's Ge'ez text (1851) and Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church printed text (EOTC); the Ethiopic manuscripts
readings.orig: ነገረ ፡ ወውእቱ ፡ ነገር ፡ ኮነ ፡ አርዌ ፡ ዐቢየ (nägärä wäwʾətu nägär konä ʾärwe ʿäbiyä)
readings.en: a word, and that word became a great beast
readings.plain: a word, and that word became a great animal

readings.w: Conjecture of R. H. Charles (1912; his English of 1917): Hebrew מִלָּה millah "word" misread for טָלֶה taleh "lamb"
readings.orig: (Hebrew טָלֶה taleh)
readings.en: a lamb, and that lamb became a great beast
readings.plain: a lamb, and that lamb became a great animal

readings.w: Later conjecture: Hebrew רְאֵם re'em "wild ox," written in Greek letters (rēm) and taken for Greek ῥῆμα rhēma "word"; preferred by several modern commentators
readings.orig: (Hebrew רְאֵם re'em)
readings.en: a wild ox, and that wild ox became a great beast
readings.plain: a wild ox, and that wild ox became a great animal

why: No Greek or Aramaic survives here, so the Plain English Translation keeps the only text that exists. Both corrections are guesses about a lost Hebrew or Aramaic original. "Lamb" fits the many lambs of 90:6–9 and appeals to Christian readers (Revelation 5:6); "wild ox" fits the cattle of the vision and the great horns that follow (compare Numbers 23:22; Deuteronomy 33:17). Ethiopian Orthodox readers hold to "word" and read it of Christ (John 1:1, 14).

a: Four came out of that place
p: Both Ge'ez texts say "one" came out, and three with him. The story needs "four."

readings.w: Reading required by 88:1, 88:3 and 89:1 ("one of those four") and by the seven of 90:21; Charles's English
readings.orig: (Ge'ez numeral ፬, four)
readings.en: four came out from that place, and three with them
readings.plain: Four came out of that place

readings.w: Dillmann's Ge'ez text (1851) (numeral ፩) and Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church printed text (EOTC) (አሐዱ)
readings.orig: ወ፩ወጽአ ፡ እምውእቱ ፡ መካን ፡ ወ፫ምስሌሁ (wä[1]wäṣʾä ʾəmwəʾtu mäkan wä[3]məslehu)
readings.en: and one came out from that place, and three with him
readings.plain: One came out of that place

why: Both texts read here have "one," but the rest of the vision speaks of "those four who came out first" (88:1, 88:3; 89:1, where Dillmann's own numeral is ፬) and of seven white ones (90:21). The Ge'ez numerals ፩ (1) and ፬ (4) are easily confused, so "one" is probably a copying slip. Whether any Ethiopic manuscript reads "four" here has not been checked for this page; the Plain English Translation follows the sense the story requires, as Charles does.

a: with her came two more calves
p: Both Ge'ez texts say "another calf." The story needs two, Cain and Abel.

readings.w: Reading the story requires (Cain and Abel are both born, 85:3–6); Charles's English ("two bulls")
readings.orig: (Ge'ez ክልኤ kəlʾe, "two")
readings.en: with her came out two calves
readings.plain: with her came two more calves

readings.w: Dillmann's Ge'ez text (1851) and Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church printed text (EOTC)
readings.orig: ወምስሌሃ ፡ ወጽአ ፡ ካልእ ፡ ጣዕዋ (wämsəleha wäṣʾä kalʾ ṭaʿwa)
readings.en: with her came out another calf
readings.plain: with her came another calf

why: Read strictly, "another calf" with "one of them black, one red" would make the cow herself one of the colored calves. But 85:5–6 keep the cow apart from both the black and the red calf. The Ge'ez words for "another" (ካልእ kalʾ) and "two" (ክልኤ kəlʾe) look and sound alike, so the Plain English Translation takes "two," with Charles.

a: They were among those calves and cattle, grazing with them, in among them.
p: Dillmann: the stars were among the calves and cattle. EOTC: they became cattle among the calves.

readings.w: Dillmann's Ge'ez text (1851)
readings.orig: ወማእከለ ፡ እልኩ ፡ ጣዕዋ ፡ ወአልህምት ፡ ኮኑ ፡ ምስሌሆሙ (wämaʾkälä ʾəlku ṭaʿwa wäʾälhəmt konu məslehomu)
readings.en: and among those calves and cattle they were with them
readings.plain: They were among those calves and cattle, grazing with them, in among them.

readings.w: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church printed text (EOTC); Charles's English
readings.orig: ወማእከለ፡ እልኩ፡ ጣዕዋ፡ ወአልሕምተ፡ ኮኑ (wämaʾkälä ʾəlku ṭaʿwa wäʾälḥəmtä konu)
readings.en: and among those calves they became cattle
readings.plain: Among those calves they became cattle, grazing with them, in among them.

why: The difference is one ending: Dillmann's ʾälhəmt (cattle, as subject) against the EOTC's ʾälḥəmtä (cattle, as what they became). Both make sense, and 86:4 works either way. The Plain English Translation follows Dillmann's text, which it follows throughout unless there is reason not to. The EOTC reading, that the stars took the shape of bulls, is attractive, since in 86:4 they act like bulls. The Aramaic 4Q207 covers this verse, according to Milik, but its reading has not been checked for this page.

p: Both Ge'ez texts say "while he trembled." Charles's English says "without his being terrified."

readings.w: Dillmann's Ge'ez text (1851) and Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church printed text (EOTC)
readings.orig: እንዘ ፡ ይርዕድ (ʾənzä yərʿəd)
readings.en: while he trembled
readings.plain: while he trembled

readings.w: Charles's English (1912/1917); the manuscript basis of his reading has not been checked for this page
readings.en: without his being terrified
readings.plain: without his being afraid

why: The Plain English Translation follows both Ge'ez texts. Charles may have followed manuscripts with a negative, or read the phrase differently; his apparatus was not available here. Fear before an angel's message is common in the Bible (Daniel 8:17; Luke 1:12), so the Ge'ez makes good sense.

a: And there rose up sheep to lead them, all of them
p: Both Ge'ez texts say "all" of them. Charles's English says "the two sheep."

readings.w: Dillmann's Ge'ez text (1851) and Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church printed text (EOTC)
readings.orig: ወቆሙ ፡ አባግዕ ፡ ኲሎሙ ፡ እለ ፡ ይመርሕዎሙ (wäqomu ʾäbagʿ kʷilomu ʾəlä yəmärḥəwomu)
readings.en: and all the sheep who would lead them arose
readings.plain: And there rose up sheep to lead them, all of them

readings.w: Charles's English (1912/1917); the manuscript basis of his reading has not been checked for this page
readings.en: there arose the two sheep as leaders
readings.plain: And there rose up two sheep to lead them

why: The Plain English Translation follows both Ge'ez texts. Charles's "two" has been taken as Joshua and Caleb (Numbers 14:6–9). The Ge'ez "all" may mean the leaders of the generation who entered the land, with Joshua at their head.
